Thank you so much. Thank you all for your testimony. I just want to make sure that Rebecca Ahn is not here. Okay. Thank you.

Okay. The next panel will be Adrian Cacho and Christopher Leon Johnson.

Uh, yeah, hello, my name is Christopher Leon Johnson. Thank you, Chair Hudson for doing this hearing. Um, I'm calling on the City Council to call for the MTA to remove the household, um, household requirement, uh, provision within the MTA Fair Fares program. Um, I wanna know why that these so-called nonprofits such as Riders Alliance had not said not one thing about telling the MTA to remove the household requirements that really hinders a lot of families. That household requirement, um, really holds, like, really makes it where the families that really need those, um, Fair Fares can't even get the, um, can't even get the Fair Fares. Because you make, if you make a certain amount of money and you have 4 people in your house, you can't even get the— you're not eligible for the program. And I'm gonna say this right now, that a lot of people said that we need, we need to expand the Fair Fares but the thing is that the Mayor's office, they don't have— they, they say they don't have the money, but they have the money. They don't want to because

we have a mayor that's scared of the governor, and we have a mayor that's scared of Janet Lieber. But I'm gonna say this right now, I said it's the best plum outside, and I'm gonna say this right now on the record, that the, um, New York City Council need to make— need to call the mayor's office to remove the NYPD from helping out the Eagle Team when it comes to fare evasion in one of the most— in some of the most impoverished districts in New York City, such as the South Bronx, the BX12, and such as the B46, which is in, um, Crown Heights, Bedford-Stuyvesant, and the BA2 bus, which covers Canarsie and, um, Coney Island. But the Riders' Alliance is not gonna say anything about that. I told them, I said, you know why? Because they're so captive to, to, to General Lieber, they're so scared of losing that access to General Lieber. That's all they care about. Um, and I'm gonna say this right now, that, uh, going forward, like I said, we could— I say we need to make the buses faster and free. The only way— the mayor had the power to do it. He just don't want to do it. He's just scared of doing it. He's scared of MTA TWU, and he's scared of the MTA, um, bosses, Jim Lieber. I'm not scared. I'm not scared of them.

I'm getting in their face, telling them in their face what they need to— I'll tell them about themselves. But like I said, going forward, like I said, the City Council, what they need to do is make— introduce a bill to bar the NYPD from helping out MTA Eagle Team for enforcing fare evasion. I think that needs to go forward with the City Council if they really care about the poor in those districts, because that's a big hinderer with the people over there. Thank you so much. Enjoy your day.
Thank you.

Good afternoon, everyone. So my name is Adrian Cacho, senior organizer at Open Plans, where we promote people-first street culture that prioritizes community, active mobility, and connection. Thank you to Speaker Menin, Chair Hudson, Chair Abreu, and all the committee members for holding this hearing today and for continuing to prioritize expanding this program to improve equitable access to affordable transit for hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers. So I was at the rally earlier, and we heard stories from folks about their experiences with the Fair Fares program and how important it is to them.

And we've heard stories just now from those— from these same folks. And it should be clear by now how instrumental this program is not just in making transit affordable, but also in expanding access to job opportunities and education across the city. If done right, the Fair Fares program can also deliver faster commutes to millions of subway, bus, paratransit, and commuter railroad riders in New York City right now, transforming how people get around. A lot of what we hear from our communities is not just about the lack of investment in our public spaces but also about how hard it can be to get to them. And the standard fare can add up quickly, especially for low-income families, older adults, and essential workers who are already facing high costs of living. The overlap between affordable transit and safer streets shows up in countless ways across the city. Most New Yorkers rely on public transit to get around, and we must maintain this accessibility, which in turn keeps our streets less congested and easier to navigate. This is why we must expand the Fair Fares program, expand the eligibility up to 300% of the federal poverty level, and reduce

administrative burdens so that more New Yorkers can utilize this program. Thank you.
Thank you so much for your testimony. We will now move to virtual testimony. Please wait for your name to be called to testify, and please select unmute when prompted. Charlton D'Souza.

You may begin. CHARLTON D’SOUZA: Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Charlton D'Souza. I'm the president of Passengers United. We're a 501 C3 nonprofit, and we support, uh, all the proposals for Fair Fares but I want to bring some issues. So a lot of minimum wage earners, they make like close to $40,000 a year, and they— the, that threshold should be $40,000 to qualify for Fair Fares up to that amount. Because right now a lot of people are struggling in New York City. They cannot afford mass transit, and the MTA lied to you guys. So a lot of the empty kiosks in the customer service centers are iPads that can actually be tampered with. They're in front of the public, and most of them are broken at stations. So a lot of times the station agents cannot help people qualify for Fair Fares. Um, I also want to,

uh, point out that I could not find information on when an enrollment term starts and ends, or what the year is, on the, uh, Fair Fares website. And also, like, they need to get rid of the household income criteria for Fair Fares. That is ridiculous. Um, and, you know, the station agents are not properly trained on Fair Fares at customer service centers. But I will say this: why is it that the MTA cannot allow Fair Fares to come inside the, uh, cab summons office in Brooklyn where people have to— you know, when they get arrested or when they get a citation for fare evasion, they should be a Fair Fares officer there so people can just apply for Fair Fares there as well. Because then you would get a lot of the people who are struggling with poverty, um, and that is a big issue. And then the other issue that I want to raise is I want to thank David Jones from Community Service Society. He is an MTA board member, and he was the one who really got Fair Fares going, um, and we at Passengers United, we're a nonprofit. Fair Fares has never reached out to us.—

Thank you, your time expired.

CHARLTON D’SOUZA: Nothing. Yeah, alright, thank you.
Thank you so much. Iman Rahmani-Doster.
You may begin.

Hi, thank you so much. My name is Iman Rahmani-Doster, and I'm a senior community organizer for the Disability Justice Program for New York Lawyers for the Public Interest. And, uh, thank you so much for allowing me to uh, present my testimony today. Public transportation is a lifeline for New Yorkers with disabilities. Many disabled New Yorkers are on fixed incomes, making this lifeline difficult to afford, which is why Fair Fares is vitally important. People may think $3 isn't a lot of money, but if they only receive $900 a month in benefits and have a ton of other expenses and no support, $3 can be a lot. I remember being on a fixed income and how not only that there were times that I had to scrape together pennies to use Access-A-Ride back when it was $2.25, but I'd also have to skip vital appointments and meetings because I did not always have those pennies to scrape together.

When the city initially introduced Fair Fares, it was not available to Access-A-Ride users. New York Lawyers for the Public Interest advocated for and secured the extension of the discount program for Access-A-Ride but the benefits, um, that Fair Fares provides to Access-A-Ride is still too limited, as it only covers low-income individuals under 65, as has been mentioned earlier. Accordingly, we call on the city to remove the age cap from the Fair Fares program so that Access-A-Ride users over the age of 65 can qualify. Further, not only should this hearing have, uh, captions available on the Zoom option but also according to what I heard a couple— at a couple of other town halls that included disabled New Yorkers, they still don't even know about Fair Fares. I also appreciate the Council Members bringing up how nasty some of the HRA staff have been. Um, but the HRA folks didn't respond to that, and so I'm hoping that that can also be worked on because I think that some people don't wanna be disrespected and dehumanized in some of these offices, like I was. Additionally, Fair Fares cannot be used on the city's express buses, which cost—
Thank you, your time expired.
Thank you so much.
Thank you so much. Eric McClure.
You may begin.

Thank you, Chair Hudson. I appreciate you and Chair Abreu for holding this hearing today. My name is Eric McClure. I am the executive director of StreetsPAC. We join transit riders and our many colleagues in advocacy, including Riders Alliance and the Permanent Citizens Advisory Committee, today in calling for the expansion of the Fair Fares program to 300% of the federal poverty level, fully free transit for families earning less than 150% of the FPL, the inclusion in the program of express buses and the commuter railroads, automatic enrollment of qualified participants, and the closing of loopholes for seniors and disabled riders. While we're very supportive of Mayor Mamdani's efforts to make the city buses fast and free, it's clear that it will take time to fully realize the elimination of bus fares. And the fact is that about two-thirds of Fair Fares use is on the subways.

While a $3 transit fare may seem trivial to some, the cost to commute regularly to work or to make other necessary trips adds up quickly. The Community Service Society reports that 1 in 5 New Yorkers struggle to pay transit fares. Working-class New Yorkers are too often forced to choose between paying for a bus or subway ride or paying for a meal or, uh, another vital expense. And the expansion of the Fair Fares program as outlined will save more than 2 million New Yorkers nearly $1,000 a year. We strongly support Committee on General Welfare Chair Hudson's Intro 248, which would require creation of a system to automatically enroll eligible, uh, people in city-operated benefits like Fair Fares. Automatic enrollment would increase participation in the Fair Fares program significantly, eliminating the need to complete a laborious enrollment process that creates an unnecessary barrier to usage. We're also highly supportive of expanding Fair Fares coverage to the MTA's express buses and commuter railroads, which would be especially helpful to people who live in parts of the city that aren't well served or served at all by the subway system.

Similarly, we support the closing of program loopholes like the age cutoff for Access-A-Ride, which forces qualified participants to start paying the full fare when they turn 65. We're well aware of the fiscal headwinds the city faces today, but a relatively modest investment in a robustly expanded Fair Fares program will vastly improve the lives of the most impoverished New Yorkers, and unlocking their economic potential by lowering or eliminating barriers to mobility will benefit everyone in New York City.
Thank you, your time expired.
Thank you so much. I, I clocked your speed reading there Eric, thank you. Uh, Ramona Ferreira.
You may begin.

Good afternoon. Um, Fair Fares is a lifeline and equalizer for New Yorkers. Uh, as, like, myself, uh, this program makes it possible for me to engage the city fully. Without it, I would not access to medical, social, and cultural activities. It would also limit my civic participation. I am a tenant organizer within public housing and attend NYCHA developments, um, for meetings where they are

facing privatization. This is something that is allowed under public housing rights and encouraged. Each meeting, I meet tenants that have heard about the harms caused by privatization of public housing only through other tenants. NYCHA hides from tenants the statistics on eviction and displacement, increases in rent, and doesn't tell them how their federally protected rights and benefits under the PAC program, um, would actually harm them. So instead, uh, we are promised new appliances and flooring, but for those of us trying to save public housing, we know better and we show up, um, while not getting paid to do so. So this mayor actually wants to not only stop the expansion of Fair Fares, but also wants to privatize public housing further by allocating $662 million towards PAC. He's also supporting the demolition of 18 buildings in Chelsea, and tenants will have to continue to fight against him and his budget and will continue to depend on public transportation to do so, all while not getting paid to do this work. So I urge the Council to shift all funding away from privatization of public housing and towards

Section 9 comprehensive modernization, and we urge you to automatically enroll folks in Fair Fares and expand the program.

Thank you so much. Thank you to everyone who's testified. If there's anyone present in the room or on Zoom that has not had the opportunity to testify, please raise your hand. Are you Norm Miller? Okay, great. We can call you up to the dais. Apologies, I called you twice before, but I don't think you were in the room. Okay, no problem. You're on.

Alright, good afternoon, Transportation Committee. My name is Norm Miller. I am a student at CUNY's New York City College of Technology, which is City Tech, which is right on the opposite side of the Brooklyn Bridge, located in downtown Brooklyn. I am also, um, part of the New York Public Interest Research Group, also known as NYPIRG. I'm also on the student board of directors. Um, I just wanna say that I am a full-time undergraduate, and being a full-time undergrad comes with a lot of financial burden, as I have to struggle between paying for transportation, $24 a week, and paying for tuition every semester. Having a— sorry.

Having a program such as Fair Fares can help alleviate that burden. It can give opportunities for jobs and education and a better quality of life. People ages— people between 16 and 64 years of age qualify for Fair Fares, but only under $375,000 people are enrolled. Transit costs should never be a blockade for either— for education or, or opportunities. I'm also— I'm calling on the expansion of Fair Fares so that more low-income and more working-class New Yorkers can get 50% discounts on buses, subways, paratransits, and the MTA's two commuter railroad systems, the Long Island Railroad and Metro North. Thank you for your time.
Thank you so much for your testimony.
You're welcome.

Okay, is there anyone else on Zoom that would like to testify? If so, please use the raise hand function. Seeing no one else, I'd like to note that written testimony, which will be reviewed in full by committee staff, may be submitted, uh, to the record up to 72 hours after the close of this hearing by

emailing it to testimony@council.nyc.gov. I wanna thank everyone again for their testimony today. I'd like to thank, uh, Chair Abreu and Speaker Menin for partnering with me on this hearing. I think it's incredibly important that we heard the testimony that we heard from folks today, specifically those who have been criminalized for poverty, uh, where, uh, Fair Fares, um, card or being in the Fair Fares program would have prevented something like that from happening. And so, uh, I'd also like to thank the Administration for coming out, and with that, I will adjourn today's hearing. Thank you.

Unpause and then this together. Testing, testing. This is a microphone check for the New York City Council Committee on Disabilities. Today’s date is May 5th, 2026. We are located in Hearing Room 1, and this is being recorded by Sergeant Ben Levy.

Good morning, welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Disabilities. Please silence all cell phones, electronic devices. Moving forward, no one is to approach the dais. If you have any questions, please reach out to the Sergeant at Arms. Chair Hanif, we are ready to begin.

[GAVEL] Good morning, everyone. I'm Council Member Shahana Hanif, Chair of the Committee on Disabilities. Thank you for your patience this morning. Apologies for being late. I'm in my mid-30s, brown woman, wear black glasses, and I have cur— wavy, medium-sized hair. Today I am wearing a white shawl, white shirt, black blazer, and I'm seated behind a dais. Welcome to our oversight hearing on equal economic opportunity for New Yorkers with disabilities. Nearly 1 in 6 New York City residents has a

disability. Of those who are working age, only 41% are employed compared to 81% of non-disabled New Yorkers. That gap is not a product of individual limitations. It's the product of structural barriers that we have allowed to persist. Employer discrimination, inaccessible workplaces, a benefit system that can punish people for working, and a workforce infrastructure that was not built with people with significant disabilities in mind. The city has made commitments. In 2023, the Adams Administration announced the plan to advance career success for people with disabilities with a goal of connecting 2,500 New Yorkers with disabilities to employment by July 2026. More than $10 million in city funds has been committed. By the end of last year, nearly 1,700 individuals had been connected to employment, and 2 months remain. These placements are important. Every one of them represents a New Yorker who cleared real barriers to get to work, and the agencies and mayoral offices in this room deserve credit for that. They— the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities New

York City at Work program has earned international recognition, including the Zero Project Award for innovative policies in employment. And its trainers have lived this. At the city's Workforce One career centers, the Department of Small Business Services SCION team has established a baseline for inclusive delivery that did not exist before. The Office of Talent and Workforce Development's Center for Workplace Accessibility and Inclusion launched the city's first-of-its-kind digital accessibility training in partnership with Microsoft equipping city employees to create content that works for everyone. And last month, the New York City Talent and the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity, alongside MOPED and SBS, did something this city has never done before. They awarded $7.5 million for employment programs that will be co-designed by New Yorkers with disabilities themselves. Not for them, with them. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed into law last July will reduce federal Medicaid spending by more than $1 trillion over 10 years. The services that allow people with significant disabilities to live independently— home health aides, personal care

services, day programs— are among the first things states cut when federal revenues contract. Without those services, employment is not a realistic goal. The city's workforce programs are downstream of that infrastructure. Their effectiveness depends on it. At the same time, the Social Security Administration has lost more than 7,500 employees since January of last year. Disability insurance appeal backlogs have grown by more than 73,000 cases in a single year. Average processing times for disability claims can exceed 200 days. For a New Yorker trying to decide whether they can enter the workforce without losing their benefits, that uncertainty is not a minor inconvenience. It is a reason not to try. Last week, the City Comptroller's Office hosted a disability justice roundtable and committed to publishing an annual economic snapshot on disability employment in the city. And last December, the Comptroller's Office reported that 725,000 New York City Medicaid enrollees stand to lose coverage through new federal work reporting and recertification requirements, and that 230,000 more

New York City residents will lose no-cost essential plan coverage as early as July 1st of this year. These are not abstract federal policy questions. So today we are asking straightforward questions. Is the city's current investment commensurate with the scale of need? Are the city's programs reaching New Yorkers with intellectual, developmental, and psychiatric disabilities, or primarily those who are already closest to employment ready? As federal benefits become less reliable and harder to access, is the city equipped to help its own program participants navigate that uncertainty and stay in the workforce? And what is the Administration's plan for supporting equal economic opportunity for New Yorkers with disabilities after July 2026? Employment is not a privilege for New Yorkers with disabilities, it is a civil rights issue. One that touches housing, healthcare, food security, and the ability to participate fully in civic life. We will not get this right by treating it as a workforce development problem alone. We have to be honest about the structural barriers that remain, the federal threats that are bearing down on us, the gap

between what is being promised and what has been delivered. Thank you to the Administration for being here today, as well as the disability advocates, service providers, and members of the public who have traveled to testify or submitted written testimony. Your presence here is an act of self-advocacy, and we do not take it for granted. Thank you to all the staff who made today's hearing possible, including Disabilities Committee staff, Senior Legislative Counsel Sarah Sucher, and Senior Legislative Policy Analyst Chloe Rivera. I also wanna recognize any Council Members who are here. Anybody on the Zoom? No. Okay, all right, they're missing out on a- on a great hearing. Um, and now I will pass the mic to Committee Counsel to administer the oath to members of the Administration prior to their testimony.

Will you please raise your right hand and respond verbally with I do? Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these Committee Members and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Thank you. You may begin your testimony when ready.
Hello. Can you hear me? Okay, good. Um, good morning, um, Chair Hanif.
You might need to bring it a little closer. I think that—

Okay, I figured. Is this better? Yeah. Okay. Um, good morning, Chair Hanif, um, and Members of the Committee, um, will join hopefully later, um, and to the audience as well. Um, thank you for the opportunity to speak, uh, to you today. Uh, my name is Nisha Agarwal, the Commissioner of the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities. I have short black hair and brown skin. I'm wearing a navy top and slacks. Um, I have aphasia and I have my handy cane somewhere around. Mhm. Um, MOPD or MOPD's mission is to ensure that, uh, New York City is accessible and inclusive for the more than 1 million New Yorkers with disabilities who live and work in this city. We do direct services, um, community engagement, strategic communication, and policymaking at the local, state, national, and international level for both public and private stakeholders. And employment, um, employment, um, for people with disabilities is vital. Um, first I will walk

through the, uh, setting of the scene, um, with some numbers. In employment for New York City, just 40% of New Yorkers with disabilities of working age are employed compared to 73% of city, uh, uh, overall working age population. And for those who are in the labor force, the employment rate is, um, nearly double, 13% for people with disabilities compared to, um, 7% citywide. We also know that on average, um, people with disabilities may spend, um, approximately 20% of their income on disability-related expenses, um, causing a strain to their incomes. I agree on that. Um, furthermore, people with disabilities grapple with a tight, um, housing market, inflation costs on food and other necessities, um, transportation barriers, health care coverage considerations, and, um, other everyday affordable, um, matters. The bottom line is people with disabilities are feeling the burden of affordability issues, um, oftentimes more exacerbated, um, rates than, uh, compared to other New Yorkers. A core, uh, focus of our work, um, is, ah, about jobs with people with disabilities, the dignity of their work, the independence that it could provide,

and the, um, ability to build a life in the city that we all love. For example, um, MOPD's signature job initiative NYC@Work has been active for more— about a decade. And it provides a continuum of individual services to both job seekers and job, uh, employers. For job seekers, we offer career advice, um, uh, resume and in— interview, uh, preparation, uh, guidance on disclosure and reasonable accommodations, retention services and, um, supports for those who apply to city government. On the employer side, we provide recruitment, uh, support, pre-screening, uh, candidate, uh, referrals, and, um, personalized hiring events, among other things. To date, um, our program has helped 800 New Yorkers with disabilities secure employment. Including a significant number of people, um, who did 55A programs, a pathway for, um, people with disabilities to secure, um, employment with the city. And since, uh, July 2023, in conjunction with our sister agencies, um, we, uh, completed more than 3,000 people with disabilities have secured employment. Um, nearly, uh, 150 were from, uh, New York City at work. While MOPD has been at the forefront of this, uh, work, we cannot do it, uh,

without the partnerships with our city agencies, um, and our colleagues, um, uh, who are also committed to this effort, and they are all seated at the dais today. Um, finally, I want to share a success story so that we can all put this in perspective. When asked what, uh, what one of our colleagues, um, liked about his job, he said, "My work feels meaningful." He went on to provide advice to other job seekers, uh, saying, "Be patient. The right opportunity will come your way." This, uh, client now works on health and, uh, safety issues at DCAS. He has a background in project analytics and has a degree, uh, background in, uh, uh, transportation-related issues. He came to one of our job, um, fairs in 2024 and, uh, provided through a whole year of, of, um, period after a, a soft job possibility, um, translated into a tangible employment. He was also able to use, um, the 55A program as a pathway to, uh, employment with the city. He has a learning disability and one of his goals is to be more— is to build his confidence in the workplace.

To that end, um, one of our career advisors, um, has used to— has, uh, continued to work with this client while he, uh, still works in DCAS. They are debriefing about everyday issues that the client faces, ways to build his confidence in his unit, and shape his ongoing career trajectory. That, um, ongoing support for our career advisors continues for a year, uh, beyond the employment, and our, uh, advisor and the client have been, uh, have been talking consistently for 8 months now. This is just one story of a job seeker that has been touched by working with, um, At Job, uh, program, and, um, showing the dedication of our, our staff and the powerful story of how patience, support, connection, and follow-up can impact all New Yorkers, including New Yorkers with disabilities. Um, our goal, um, working together and fighting to extend opportunities for people with disabilities, just highlighted, um, above here. Um, this matters, um, to everyone, and, um, thank you very much for the opportunity to testify today, and I, um, am happy to answer any questions. Thank you.

Good morning. Good morning, Chair Hanif and any members that do join us, uh, at this

hearing. My name is Haris Khan, Chief of Staff at the New York City Department of Small Business Services. I'm pleased to join today's hearing with Commissioner Agarwal from the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities, Executive Director Lipari from the Office of Talent and Workforce Development, and Assistant Commissioner Outar from the Department of Citywide Administrative Services. Per the City Controller's 2024 report, New York City working age adults with disabilities face an employment rate of just 41%, compared to 81% for those without disabilities, a gap that carries real consequences for economic security and quality of life. At SBS, doing our part to close that gap is a priority. We're committed to delivering economic opportunity for all New Yorkers, and today I want to report on the steps we're taking to better serve New Yorkers with disabilities. Over the past several years, SBS has worked to make our Workforce One Career Centers more accessible and effective for job seekers with disabilities. Through the state-funded New York Systems Change and Inclusive Opportunities Network program, or SCION,

we've expanded employee trainings, hosted targeted recruitment events, and improved accessibility across our centers. In October last year, to mark National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we hosted 3 resource fairs that connected more than 180 job seekers to community resources, benefits counseling, and job placement support. This month, we're continuing that momentum with 2 additional events, one tomorrow in Jamaica, Queens, another on May 12th in Staten Island. Across all of our Workforce One career centers, we've placed more than 1,200 New Yorkers with disabilities into jobs since 2024, and more than 150 Workforce One Center staff members have received training and support from our disability resource coordinators, as well as disability etiquette awareness training from our colleagues at MOPD. This ensures that when a New Yorker with disability walks through any of our doors, they're met by- they're met by staff who are prepared to serve them with competence and respect. Our DRCs also work directly with job seekers to help them navigate disability benefits, connect them to

independent living centers, and refer them to DCWP financial counselors that are co-located in our 5 borough-based hub centers. Additionally, we've embedded MOPD's NYC at Work program within our downtown Brooklyn Workforce One Center at 9 Bond Street, deepening the range of direct service available to New Yorkers with disabilities at that location. Looking ahead, SBS is pleased to share that in partnership with MOPD, NYC Talent, NYC Opportunity, the city announced awards for an innovative co-design pilot program on April 1st, 2026. This initiative invests $7.5 million over the next 4 years to support providers in designing and implementing accessible workforce programs with people with disabilities at the table as collaborators in program design and not just recipients of services. SVS is proud to contribute contract and program management support to this effort. Decisions about vendor selection, training models, and program direction are also informed by NYC Opportunity as the funder, NYC Talent as the citywide coordinating

entity on workforce development, and MOPD as the citywide subject matter expert on disability. Together, we expect this initiative will generate meaningful learnings for this field over the next 4 years. We thank Council for the opportunity to testify today and welcome any questions.

You're supporting Bill H303? And ask that— do not support this bill! Do you know people with disabilities are gonna be placed in nursing homes? Like, I was threatened to be placed into a nursing home. Ah, hmm, mhm, like, you know, I mean, mm-hm, just take one second. Sorry. What happened?
You can testify, and I'd love to hear this. So could— are you okay to wait to be able to testify?

We've been trying to reach you, you know, regarding this, and we have reached a wall. Um, it seems like the city council is hell-bent on passing this bill, that it's going to ace tomorrow and it's probably going to be voted for on, on the 14th, uh, and no one seems to understand that this bill does not do what it, uh, is supposed to, you know.
I'd love to hear this in full, and I'd love to— love for you to stay here. So let's continue this during the testimony section.
I remember being with her in the round table at MOPD given, you know, and I was glad that you were the chosen as the disability Chair, but you being on this bill, you know, while people—

If- I'd love to continue this, so, and I don't want to get you out of the room um, so please respect just the decorum right now so that we can have this conversation during the testimony section of this hearing. I do not want to get you out of the room.
People with disabilities to your office that we get ignored, we have no choice but—

I understand that. Thank you. Okay, so starting with the plan to advance career success for people with disabilities, I'd like to, uh, ask a few questions. What is the Mamdani Administration's assessment of the inherited plan? And what is working, what is not, and what, if anything, is going to change?

Good morning. My name is Douglas Lipari. I'm the Executive Director of the

Office of Talent and Workforce Development, or NYC Talent for short. I'm a white male with brown hair, a beard, and wearing a blue suit and a white shirt and a reddish-pinkish tie. We are absolutely committed to making sure that there is opportunity for all New Yorkers to be connected to employment pathways and have, uh, our employers here in the city of New York have access to the talent. And that talent includes people with disabilities. And so, um, it is core to the work of our office at NYC Talent to make sure that people with disabilities are connected to job opportunities.
